# Education in Poland
Education in Poland begins with compulsory primary school (szkoła podstawowa), which lasts eight years and typically starts at age six or seven; the previous system of 6-year primary followed by 3-year junior high (gimnazjum) was abolished in 2017. After primary school, students enter upper secondary education, which includes several pathways: general secondary schools (liceum) for those seeking the "Matura" exam and entry to higher education; technical schools (technikum) for vocational and technical training, offering access to the Matura as well; and basic vocational schools (zasadnicza szkoła zawodowa), which provide practical skills and a certificate that can be supplemented for university entry. Mentally or physically handicapped students may attend special schools that also prepare for the Matura.
For tertiary education, Poland employs the Bologna scheme, with most higher education structured in two cycles: a three-year bachelor's degree followed by a two-year master's degree, and some fields offering long-cycle master's programs (for example, medicine). Doctoral programs typically take around three years. Grading at universities uses a numeric scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (highest), often with 0.5 point increments. Language instruction in schools includes one or two foreign languages, with English and German being the most common. Historically, Poland established early ministries and universities and has maintained high educational standards through multiple reforms.
